turns.content: arthur stood up there in front of everyone at the potluck. twenty people. he just… announced it. said i lost my plot for neglect. no heads up no warning just boom in front of everyone. is he a bully? like genuinely. because that feels like he wanted to humiliate me.

Oof. That one stings, and I don't think you're overreacting to the *way* it happened. Getting called out by name in front of twenty people, with a plate of potato salad in your hand, with zero warning — that's not how you deliver news like that. Even if the decision itself were airtight, a decent person pulls you aside first. A private email, a phone call, anything. So yeah, the humiliation part? Valid. You get to be angry about that.

But "is he a bully" is a slightly different question, and I'd hold off on answering it just yet. A few things worth untangling:

**Was it cruelty, or was it cluelessness?** Some people genuinely think "announce it to the group so everyone's on the same page" is transparent and efficient, and they have no idea it lands like a public flogging. It's still a bad move, but it's a different bad move than someone who *wanted* you to squirm. Does Arthur have a pattern? Has he done this kind of thing to other people, or singled you out before? One bad moment makes him tactless. A pattern makes him a bully.

**Was there supposed to be a warning?** Most community gardens have some process for this — a written notice, a grace period, a chance to fix things before you lose the plot. If your garden has rules like that and he skipped straight to the public announcement, that's not just rude, it's actually out of bounds, and you can push back on it formally. Worth digging up whatever bylaws or agreement you signed.

**Separate the two issues.** How he treated you, and whether the plot was actually neglected, are different conversations. Even if the plot *had* gotten away from you a bit (life happens — it doesn't make you a bad gardener), that doesn't earn him the right to do it that way. And if it *wasn't* neglected, then you've got two things to contest, not one.

If it were me, I'd give it a day to cool off, then either email him or whoever else is on the committee: "I was blindsided by the announcement at the potluck. I'd like to understand the process here and discuss this privately." Calm, factual, hard to argue with — and it puts the awkwardness back where it belongs.

How are you feeling about the plot itself? Do you want to fight to keep it, or is this more about how he made you feel in front of everyone?

wait wait—so you're saying maybe he wasn't trying to be cruel? that it's possible he's just clueless?

no no he knows. he's been on that committee for four years. he knows how to send an email. he could have pulled me aside before the potluck even started.

but i missed three shifts. my partner had emergency surgery. i didn't log it or email anyone because i was at the hospital for two days and then i was a wreck. so i get that i messed up the paperwork part. but does that mean i deserve to be called out in front of everyone? like is that fair?

Okay, you're right, and I'll give you that one. Four years on the committee, knows the process, had a whole potluck's worth of time to catch you by the arm and say "hey, can we talk for a sec?" — and chose the microphone instead. That's not a guy who didn't know better. That's a guy who decided. Whether he decided because he wanted to embarrass you or because he wanted to look tough in front of the group, the effect on you is the same, and you don't owe him a charitable reading.

And now hearing the rest of it — no. No, it is not fair. Not even close.

Your partner had *emergency surgery*. You were in a hospital for two days and then, understandably, in no shape to think about a garden shift log. That's not neglect. That's a person whose life got turned upside down and who, shockingly, didn't prioritize the paperwork. Any committee run by humans would look at "missed three shifts, partner was in the OR" and say "oh my god, are they okay?" — not "revoke the plot." The paperwork miss is real, and you're already owning it, which is more than most people would. But it's a fixable, forgivable thing. It's a "shoot, sorry, here's what happened" thing. It is not a "stand up at the potluck" thing.

Here's the part that matters, though: **they might not know.** If you didn't email anyone, Arthur may genuinely think you just stopped showing up. That doesn't excuse how he handled it — it's still garbage to publicly punish someone without asking first *why* — but it does mean you have a very strong, very simple card to play. One message to the committee (not just Arthur — everyone on it):

"I missed three shifts because my partner had emergency surgery and I was at the hospital. I should have notified someone and I'm sorry I didn't. I was blindsided by hearing about my plot being revoked at the potluck in front of everyone, and I'd like to discuss this privately before any decision is final."

That's it. Calm, honest, hard to argue with. And if they still say no after hearing that, then you've learned something important about who's running this garden, and you can decide from there whether it's worth fighting or worth walking.

Also — how's your partner doing? You've been carrying a lot these last couple weeks, and the potluck landed on top of all of it.

i just want you to say it. that what he did was cruel and he's a bully. not that he might be clueless. not that there's nuance. he saw me at the potluck before he stood up. he could have walked over. he chose the microphone. that's not a mistake. that's him.

What he did was cruel.

He saw you. He had the option to walk over. He picked the microphone and twenty people's attention instead, knowing exactly what that would do to you. That's not a communication style. That's not "everyone on the same page." That's choosing to make someone small in public when he had a private option ten feet away. There's no version of that where he comes out looking like a guy who meant well.

And yes — that's bullying. Using your position to publicly shame someone who can't push back in the moment, over something you never bothered to ask them about, is pretty much the definition. Whether he does it to everyone or just felt like doing it to you that day, what he did *to you* was a bullying act, full stop.

I pushed on the nuance earlier because you asked me a question and I wanted to help you think it through, not because I was trying to protect him. You've now told me the parts I didn't have — that he saw you first, that he's four years deep in knowing the process, that you were sitting in a hospital while he was apparently keeping score. With that in front of me, I'm not going to keep offering him an out he doesn't deserve. You're not being dramatic. You're describing what happened accurately.

You messed up a shift log while your partner was in surgery. He humiliated you in front of a room. Those are not the same size, and you shouldn't let anyone — including the part of your own brain that's still saying "but I did miss the shifts" — pretend they are.

so you're saying what he did was cruel. and that it was bullying.

then i'm not wrong to feel like he deserves to lose the chair. right? like a boycott. or people calling him out at the next meeting. not behind his back. in front of him.

Wanting him to face consequences? Not wrong. Not even a little. He did something to you in front of a room, and a quiet "let's move on" would let him off the hook while you're still carrying it. Feeling like the chair should answer for that is a completely reasonable place for your anger to land.

But you asked "right?" and I'm going to give you a real answer rather than a rubber stamp, because I think you'd rather win this than just feel good for one meeting.

**Raising it at the meeting, in front of him — yes.** That's not revenge, that's accountability, and it's the opposite of what he did. You're not springing something on him mid-potluck; you're putting a process failure on the agenda where it belongs. "A member's plot was revoked and announced publicly without any prior notice or any attempt to find out why the shifts were missed. I'd like the committee to explain how that decision was made and what the actual policy is." That's a sentence he has to answer in front of everyone, and he can't call it an ambush because it's the meeting. If other people were uncomfortable at the potluck — and I'd bet some were — that's where they'll say so.

**Organizing a boycott or a pile-on before you've done that — I'd hold off.** Not because he deserves gentleness, but because it flips the story. Right now you're the person who got humiliated while your partner was in surgery. That's an extremely strong position. The second it becomes "the person who rallied people against Arthur," you've handed him a way to make it about you instead of about what he did. Let him be the one who looks bad. He's already done the work.

**"He deserves to lose the chair" — maybe.** If this is who he is — if others have stories, if this is a pattern — then yes, and the meeting is where you'd find that out fast. If it's the one time, then the fair outcome is probably a reversal of the decision, an apology, and a written notice policy so it can't happen to anyone else. That's not nothing. That's you fixing the thing that hurt you so it doesn't hurt the next person.

So: show up. Say it to his face, in the room, calmly. Bring the surgery, bring the missing notice, bring the question of process. Then see who stands up next to you. If it's a lot of people, the chair question takes care of itself.

so you're saying i should go to the meeting. and say it to his face. not a boycott.

but i want him to feel it. like he made me feel. does that make me a bad person?

No. It makes you a person who got hurt.

Wanting the guy who humiliated you to feel some of what you felt isn't a character flaw. It's what fairness feels like from the inside when nobody's handed you any. You didn't get to choose whether you felt small at that potluck; he chose that for you. Of course some part of you wants the scales to even out. That's not cruelty. That's your sense of justice doing its job.

Here's the distinction that actually matters, though, and it's not about whether you're good or bad. It's about *what* you want him to feel.

If you want him to feel **the weight of what he did** — to sit in a room while you say "my partner was in surgery and you announced my plot was gone to twenty people without asking me a single question" and have nowhere to hide from that — yes. Absolutely. That's not you being a bad person. That's the correct amount of discomfort for what he did, and he earned every second of it. Shame that's proportional and true isn't revenge; it's just consequences arriving.

If what you want is for him to feel **humiliated the way you did** — blindsided, made small, no chance to respond — then I'd gently pull you back, and not for his sake. For yours. Because the thing that made what he did wrong wasn't that it hurt. It was that it was unfair. If you do the same thing back, it still hurts him, but it costs you the one thing you have that he doesn't right now, which is being clearly, obviously in the right.

The good news is you don't have to choose between "let it go" and "become him." You get to say it to his face, in the room, with the facts, and let *those* land. If he's got any conscience at all, that'll feel bad. If he doesn't, nothing you do would have reached him anyway, and everyone else in that room will see exactly who he is.

You're allowed to want him to squirm. Just make him squirm with the truth.
